vignette:
She is 37, a touring musician who used to measure time by set lists, sound checks, and the strange comfort of airport terminals. Before the trauma, her life is noisy in a way she loves: cables underfoot, half-heard jokes backstage, the pressure of a monitor in her ear, the small electric moment before she walks into stage light. She lives with her partner between tours, writing songs at the kitchen table, tapping rhythms against coffee mugs. She has always accepted a certain amount of chaos as part of the job. Crowds are where she feels most alive.

The attack happens three years ago at an outdoor summer festival in a large city. It is late afternoon, hot enough that the metal barriers burn against people’s forearms. She is not on stage yet; she is off to one side near the artist area, talking with another performer and absently running scales under her breath. Then there is a sound she does not understand at first—too sharp to be part of the music, too close to be a technical problem. The crowd’s movement changes before her mind catches up. What had been swaying becomes pushing. Someone screams in a way she still sometimes hears when she is trying to fall asleep.

The next few minutes remain broken into vivid, disconnected pieces. A security guard shouting for everyone to get down. The smell of spilled beer, hot pavement, something metallic in the air. Her cheek pressed to the ground behind a barricade. Her phone vibrating in her pocket while she is too afraid to move. She remembers thinking, with startling clarity, that her partner would see this on the news before hearing from her. She remembers the silence after the loudness most of all, the eerie pause that comes when people are listening for the next danger.

She gets out physically unharmed. For days, this fact makes her feel she has no right to be as shaken as she is. She gives statements, answers texts, tells family members she is okay. She says the words automatically, then notices her hands trembling so badly she cannot hold a mug without using both hands. In the first weeks afterward, she does not sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. Each time she drifts off, she jerks awake with her heart racing, convinced she has heard popping sounds outside the window. In dreams, she is back on the pavement, unable to find the people she came with. Sometimes in the dream she is supposed to go onstage while the crowd runs from her.

When she returns to performing, she tells herself that routine will fix it. Instead, the things that once felt ordinary begin to seem dangerous. During sound check, a burst of feedback makes her drop to a crouch before she can stop herself. At one club, someone slams a door near the green room and she feels heat rush through her body, her vision narrowing so quickly she has to sit on the floor with her back against the wall. She becomes preoccupied with exits in every venue. Before any rehearsal or show, she scans the room and quietly counts doors, barriers, and places to hide. If a bandmate changes the setup at the last minute, she becomes irritable in a way that surprises even her.

Her partner notices the shrinking first. She stops wanting to go to concerts unless she is performing and contractually obligated to be there. She chooses smaller venues, turns down festival offers, then tells herself it is because she wants a different pace of life. She no longer stands in the middle of a crowd after a set to talk with fans; she signs quickly, smiles tightly, and retreats backstage. At restaurants she asks to sit facing the entrance. On public transit she keeps one earbud out and watches people’s hands. She used to write songs from observation, collecting fragments of strangers’ conversations. Now her attention hooks onto threat. A dropped bag, a raised voice, a person moving quickly against the flow of a crowd—each one pulls her body into alarm before her mind can reason with it.

She is frustrated by how split her life feels. On stage, she can still disappear into music for a few minutes at a time, and those moments remind her of who she was. Then a sudden flash from a phone camera or a loud crack from outside will yank her back into the festival, and afterward she feels ashamed, angry, exhausted. She tells herself she is being dramatic. She avoids interviews when they mention resilience or “getting back out there,” because the language feels false. What looks like courage from the outside often feels, to her, like careful management of panic.

Now, in the present, she describes living as if her nervous system never fully powers down. She checks locks twice before bed. She startles when her partner comes up behind her in the kitchen. She keeps her phone charged obsessively and shares her location when she leaves for a show. Some nights she sits with her guitar in the darkened living room, playing the same chord progression over and over because repetition is one of the few things that settles her breathing. She misses the easy intimacy she once felt with audiences, the sense that a crowd could hold joy instead of danger. She still performs, still writes, still loves music. But every room is entered with calculation now, every loud sound carries a shadow, and part of her remains braced for the moment ordinary life turns catastrophic again.
